description: Passionate about space, technology, AI, and creative problem-solving. Looking for teammates skilled in coding, design, research, or data who are ready to collaborate and build something awesome.
summary:
Sol 72 is a free browser game where you run a Mars or Moon outpost and keep four astronauts alive for 72 hours (a “sol” is one Martian day). Nothing needs installing, and no account is needed.

How it works. You walk around a 3D base and make nine choices, such as running the rover, growing food, sheltering from radiation, adding shielding, or switching on the generator. Every choice costs something elsewhere: sheltering protects the crew but stops the rover and lowers morale, and the generator burns fuel. A coach tip names the one thing that needs attention. Everything is built on real NASA data. Solar flares come from NASA DONKI, Mars weather from InSight, and the Earth-Mars radio delay from JPL positions. Players can face today’s Sun or real storms from 2017, 2024 and 2003. Every number is labelled LIVE, ARCHIVE or game-scaled.

The challenge it answers. Young learners rarely see the trade-offs behind real missions, only the results. Sol 72 lets them feel those trade-offs: power, life support, shielding, food, and a crew that cannot call for help in real time.
details:
SOL 72 is a free browser-based game where players manage a Mars or Moon outpost for 72 hours, keeping four astronauts alive. Players explore a 3D base and make nine key decisions, including operating the rover, growing food, managing radiation shelters, adding shielding, and generating power. Every decision involves a trade-off: shelter protects the crew but stops outside work and lowers morale.

The simulation uses real NASA data, including DONKI solar-flare records, InSight Mars weather, JPL planetary positions for communication delays, and Curiosity and Artemis radiation research. All values are labelled LIVE, ARCHIVE, or game-scaled.

Benefits and Impact: Players experience the challenges of real space missions through interactive decision-making without requiring technical knowledge. The game runs in a browser with no installation or account, making it accessible at home and in classrooms.

Tools: JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Three.js, Web Audio API, Node.js, and Playwright.

Creativity: Players can replay historical solar storms from 2017, 2024, and 2003, with different environments and difficulty levels.

Factors Considered: Scientific accuracy, transparent data labelling, balanced gameplay, accessibility, and replayability.
dataRefs: NASA DONKI: Space Weather Database (solar flares, solar energetic particles, storm records)
NASA/JPL Approximate Positions of the Planets
NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources)
NASA Curiosity RAD: Mars Radiation Measurements (Hassler et al. 2014)
NASA Artemis II: Radiation Storm Shelter and Space Weather
NASA NTRS: 2018 Global Mars Dust Storm (20190001691)
NASA Solar Cycle 25 Blog: Strong Flare, 30 June 2026
projectRefs: Chang’e-4 Lunar Lander Neutrons and Dosimetry (LND): Moon surface radiation, CNSA mission with Kiel University instrument (Zhang et al. 2020)
NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center (flare records, including the 2003 storm)
National Academies report on astronaut radiation limits, June 2021 (600 mSv career limit)
Zeitlin et al. 2013: Curiosity radiation measured on the way to Mars (press summary)
Artemis I shelter result, NASA SRAG study in Nature 2024 (CNN report)
OSD-618/640 combined space stressors study record (Data.gov)
Space.com: X8.3 solar flare of 1 Feb 2026 (flare cross-check)
Watchers: X1.9 solar flare of 18 Jan 2026 (flare cross-check)
SpaceWeatherLive: S4 radiation storm of 19 Jan 2026 (flare cross-check)
Popular Science: April 2026 solar flares (flare cross-check)
